{"number":1028,"title":"sheepdog: judge fleet freshness by stamped versions, not ref age","body":"Fixes #1025.

## The bug

`fleet-roster`'s `behind` state measured the **age of the stamped ref**. The versioned update flows deliberately never rewrite `ref`, so every member's stamp is frozen at whatever commit first vendored it — and every member's ref ages at the same rate. With the fleet stamped at `631a067` (2026-08-13) and `staleDays: 14`, the condition would have gone true for **every member at once on 2026-08-27**, opening a `fleet-drift` issue per repo for a fleet that is, by versions, current.

## What `behind` measures now

The **version gap**, and nothing else:

- stamped `engineVersion` below canon's `ENGINE_VERSION`, or
- any stamped `packVersions` entry below that pack's manifest `version` in canon,

with the gap named in the drift issue (`behind canon by engine v3 → v4, basics v5 → v7`).

Both numbers are read out of **canon** over the API — `engine/version.mjs` and each pack's `pack.mjs` — never out of the enforcer's own mount, which is itself a member and can be behind. The reader is memoized per sweep, so canon is read once per *distinct pack* across the whole walk rather than once per member.

Two shapes the classifier refuses to guess at: a pack canon has retired has no manifest to be behind and contributes no gap (an absent number never reads as zero), and a manifest that is present but whose version can't be parsed **throws**, which becomes `unknown` for that member and fails the run.

A stamp carrying neither number is `behind` by construction — an engine that stamps always stamps.

## What is unchanged

`no-stamp`, `no-scheduler` and `ref-not-on-trunk` all read the ref for what it still honestly is, provenance. The compare call stays for the `ref-not-on-trunk` wedge (#328); only its `ahead_by` and base-commit date are no longer read.

The body marker still spells `fleet-freshness` and the `behind` state token is unchanged, so open drift issues are read rather than re-opened as `unrecorded`.

## `staleDays`

With no date measure left it governs nothing, so it is retired from `parseSheepdogConfig`, from the report header, from the drift issue body and from the docs. An enforcer config still carrying the key is read, not rejected — unknown keys were always ignored.

## Also

- `packs/sheepdog/pack.mjs` version 7 → 8 (delivery signal).
- `task.md`'s "the one assumption" section rewritten; its pointer to the closed #786 removed.
- `RULES.md`'s "judging whether a member is behind" bullet no longer claims `staleDays` governs a legacy measure.

## Verification

- New tests written first and watched fail (the module had no `canonVersions` export), then green.
- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` on the rebased head: 2131 pass, 1 fail — `engine-pack-lane-shims`, which fails identically on a stashed tree ("this checkout is too shallow to walk origin/main's pack history").
- `check_the_work`: clean. `check_the_world`: 0 blocking, and the one advisory this change introduced (`task-phase-discipline`) was removed by rewording rather than waived.
- Rebased onto `cae5273` after #1013 landed; its `prework` → `code_work` rename conflicted with the `staleDays` removal on one README line, both sides kept.

{"number":1013,"title":"Rename the code phase to code-work, and stop calling tasks scheduled-only","body":"Closes #1012.

Two owner corrections to the task vocabulary. 135 files, all mechanical except the five compatibility surfaces called out below.

## 1. `prework` → `code_work` / `agentic-work`

A task's two phases are peers. The first runs deterministic code in the executor; the second runs an agent; a task may declare only the first, and many do. `prework` named it for what follows it — the same framing error the 2026-08-06 rename set out to fix and did not: `agent_preprocessing` made the agent the reference point, and `prework` kept it there, just implicitly.

Moved together: declaration fields (`prework` → `code_work`, `prework_timeout` → `code_work_timeout`), engine modules, the check, the wire word, symbols, tests and prose.

## 2. A cadence is one way an occurrence is created, not what a task is

`manual` is a first-class frequency, and work that fires on an event or a force reads the same contract as work that fires nightly. [`packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/vigilant-thompson-isx746/packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md) said "recurring" where it meant "the repo's own", and its cron rule offered the task conversion only to work that already had a cron — so event-driven work read as out of scope. It now says the conversion applies with or without a cadence, and the Actions-only exception is narrowed to the step that genuinely needs the Action's own privileges rather than the whole job.

## The five compatibility surfaces

Both earlier spellings stay accepted; nothing in the fleet has to move on this PR's clock.

| Surface | What it does |
|---|---|
| `normalizeTaskDeclaration` | every legacy key maps **straight to today's name**, so a declaration written for the oldest vocabulary normalizes in one pass rather than chaining |
| `task-declaration-shape` | reports two legacy generations rather than one, each with its own exact rename. This finding is the durable driver for member local packs — which is why neither rename ships a migration note |
| run-record wire word | `code-work`, kebab because the line format's charset (`[a-z-]+`) never admitted an underscore. `preprocess` and `prework` in a job log still parse |
| usage aggregate | its counter keys are those same words and it holds rows written under the old ones. The decode renames them; without that the next encode wrote the count as `null` |
| `engine/scheduler/queue/prework-run.mjs` | kept as a re-export shim — a fielded `core` pack imports that path, and the engine and pack lanes deliver separately (#1004, #1006) |

## Verification

- Full suite: **2097 pass, 0 fail** (`node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`).
- `check_the_world`: **0 blocking, 57 advisory** — byte-identical to the same run stashed against `main`, so no finding is new.
- `engine/selftest.mjs`: 5 probes passed.
- **See-it-fail on both new guards.** Removing the shim turns `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs` red (it derives fielded imports from trunk history, and needed `--depth=200` to be meaningful — it self-guards on a shallow clone and would otherwise have passed vacuously). Disabling the counter rename writes the historical count as `[3,null,1,0,0]`; two new tests in `usage-format.test.mjs` pin it, including a row carrying both spellings at once.

## Out of scope

`engine/migrations/2026-08-06-prework-rename/` keeps its own wording — it states what that rename did, which has not changed. Its id is likewise still spelled `prework-rename` wherever it is referenced.

{"number":1008,"title":"dashboard: digests, a fleet activity read, the grid split, and what the machinery bought","body":"Four dashboard issues, one commit each.

- **#998 — the last two fleet digests.** A `digestsRepo` (+ optional `digestsPath`) names where the digest task writes; the page shows yesterday's and the day before's. A missing day is a normal state, an unreadable repo a third state.
- **#999 — a fleet activity read.** Work closed per day stacked by outcome, runs and their pass rate, and which members moved at all.
- **#1000 — the grid split.** The member grid becomes Status / Claudinite / Work under a header band; the per-task roster becomes Declared / Now / History.
- **#1001 — what Claudinite bought this fleet.** A block above every panel: completed work, how much of it ran with nobody in the loop, how much needed a person, runs passed, members converging. This week against last.

## Nothing costs a request

Every new figure comes from a read the page already makes, so #995's budget is intact:

| New field | Where it came from |
|---|---|
| last commit per member | the head-commit call the content cache is already keyed by — its date was being discarded |
| stars, archived | the repo metadata call already made |
| the repo's own CI | the runs list already fetched, filtered to non-`schedule` runs on the default branch |
| open pull requests | the issues endpoint already returns them; they were being filtered out and dropped |
| digests | two content-at-a-sha reads, immutable-cached, 404 included |

Cold cost is unchanged; the cache version is bumped to 2 because the stored shapes changed.

## What is deliberately absent

The issues asked for a few fields I did not draw, rather than approximating them:

- **rule tokens, test counts, time saved** — each needs a member's own files read;
- **conversation-log sessions** — needs a branch listing;
- **checks enforced** — no read this page makes can count them;
- **hours saved / any score** — nothing measures it, and #1001 rules it out explicitly.

The members panel names them in its own note, so a reader can see the gap rather than trust a guess. The converge figure carries no window-over-window delta either: a mount stamp holds one date, so last week's number would count members whose *last* converge happens to fall there, and a healthy fleet would read as slowing down.

## One correction to a premise

#998 describes the digest as Markdown. It is not: `packs/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-digest/task.md` mandates **plain text** despite the `.md` name (a check enforces it over the landed series), because the file is read out verbatim through a renderer that parses no markdown. So the reader here is a few rules over lines — title, sections, `• ` items, bare URLs — which is both smaller than the "headings + paragraphs + links" the issue asked for and correct for the file. A `#` heading or `- ` bullet still renders, so a hand-written brief is not punished.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2123 pass, 0 fail. 22 new tests (`activity.test.mjs`, `digest.test.mjs`, six added to `fleet.test.mjs`), each watched to fail against a deliberate mutation of the code it covers before being kept.
- `check_the_world` and `ci-work-scope`: 0 blocking.
- The page was driven in a real browser against a synthetic five-member fleet (stubbed `fetch`, nothing else touched) and every panel read back with real values — including the missing-digest day, the grouped header bands, and the Work columns.

Closes #998
Closes #999
Closes #1000
Closes #1001

{"number":1024,"title":"core: judge mount freshness by versions, not the stamped ref","body":"Closes #1023.

`packs/core/RULES.md`'s "Judging whether Claudinite is current here" told a session to read the stamp's `ref` alongside `engineVersion` and `packVersions`. `ref` no longer answers that question: the versioned flows stamp versions and nothing else (`updates/engine-update.mjs:190`, `updates/pack-update.mjs:356`), and only a full re-vendor writes `ref`/`updated` (`vendoring/apply-vendor-set.mjs:91`).

The fleet shows the cost of the old wording — every member is frozen at `ref 631a067` (2026-08-13) while carrying pack versions bumped 2026-08-18. Reading `ref` today reports the whole fleet six days stale when eleven of twelve are current: the same false-stale reading the rule was written to prevent, arriving through the other field.

`packs/sheepdog/RULES.md` already carries the corrected form for the enforcer's side ("compare `engineVersion` and `packVersions` against canon, never the age of its stamped `ref`"). This brings the member-side rule in line with it, so the two packs no longer disagree.

`core` bumps to version 7 so members receive it; `packs/core/README.md`'s rule-index row is recounted in the same change.

## Verification

- `node engine/checks/check_the_work.mjs` — clean.
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` — 0 blocking, 57 advisory, none on the touched files (all pre-existing against `origin/main`).
- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2093/2095. The two failures are unrelated to this change: `rule-index` was one of them and is now green (re-run), and `engine-pack-lane-shims` fails only because this sandbox checkout is shallow, which the test reports itself ("this checkout is too shallow to walk origin/main's pack history").

## Not in this change

The `fleet-roster` sweep still classifies members by stamped-ref age (`packs/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs:78-84`), which is the same wrong measure in code rather than prose. Filed separately rather than widened into this PR.

{"number":1062,"title":"sheepdog: name `update` where fleet-baseline's docs still said `baselining`","body":"`force-fleet-baseline.mjs` sends `FORCED_TASK = 'update'`, but six places still described the lever as waking each member's `baselining` item — a task id canon no longer carries, so a reader who dispatched `wake: baselining` by hand would get an unmatched wake and a red tick in that member.

Corrected: the module header, the run summary's footer line, the operator log line in `worker.mjs`, `task.mjs`'s contract comment, `tasks/fleet-baseline/README.md`, and the two-levers paragraph in the pack `README.md`.

Also in the same header: "a forced run bypasses baselining's precondition (the engine records it as forced)". Under the work-item queue a wake clears `Not-before` and re-readies the item, and the executor still evaluates the precondition at pick — the same cheap no-op, by the opposite mechanism.

Left alone deliberately: the `baselining` mentions in `fleet-roster/drift-issues.mjs`, `fleet-pack-seeds/`, `fleet-api.mjs` and `migrations/`, which name the retired baselining *mechanism* a legacy member may still declare rather than a task this lever wakes.

`packs/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-baseline/` — prose only in `task.mjs` and the two READMEs; in `force-fleet-baseline.mjs` and `worker.mjs` the one non-comment change each is the operator-facing summary/log string.

Verified: `check_the_world.mjs` reports 0 blocking, and `packs-tests/sheepdog/tasks/fleet-baseline/*.test.mjs` passes 16/16. The dispatch path itself was exercised live from missingbulb/Shepherd — a `REPOS=ClaudiniteCanary` fleet-baseline item fired that member at 17:59:41Z and the canary merged `Claudinite update: 3 packs upgraded` at 18:00:35Z.

{"number":1011,"title":"Design: ad-hoc requests as a mode of the task scheduler (DESIGN §16 + sim)","body":"Refs #1010. **Design + simulator only — the mechanism is not implemented yet.** Awaiting approval of §16 before touching engine code.

Rebuilt on today's `main` (16 commits, including the triage split and the code-phase rename), so the branch is now two clean commits: the pack cut that started this is gone entirely, and §16 is re-derived against the current vocabulary rather than patched over the old one.

## The shape

A marked issue becomes an ordinary work item, run by the ordinary machinery.

- **The mark** — `claude-task` on an ordinary issue, optionally `claude-model:`. Applying a label is already write-gated by GitHub, which is the first half of the security story.
- **The tick gains a fourth job, `adopt`** — beside instantiate / ready / reclaim. It creates the item (`origin:request`, qualifier `#N`, body fields `Request:` and `Model:`) and **consumes the mark** (`claude-task` → `claude-queued`). That consumption is the whole exactly-once guard: state that clears by being acted on, no history search, no watermark. Still pure label mechanics — no precondition, no signal, no judgment about who marked it.
- **A built-in engine-owned task**, `engine/implement-request` — `manual`, `expected_outcome: open-pr`, **no code-work phase**. Shipping it as a task is what keeps this from being a second mechanism: same claim lease, same single evaluation site, same at-most-once hand-off, same ceiling enforcement, same triage lanes.
- **The precondition is the security check** — issue still open and still queued; `author_association` of `OWNER`/`MEMBER`/`COLLABORATOR` on the issue, or on a comment saying `/claude go`. No code-work at all: the authorization it would have done belongs here, and with it goes the only thing that needed a code→agent data channel.
- **How a request ends** — declined closes `outcome:obsolete` (a refusal is nobody's inbox) and disarms the issue with a comment; a run that leaves a PR **parks open at `task:needs-human-approval`** and the issue moves to `claude-in-review`; a broken run parks at `task:needs-human-failure` and writes nothing, so the standing `claude-queued` both parks it for a person and stops the next tick adopting a second run.

Two contract additions, both argued in §16.4 and §16.7: `precondition(signals, config, item)` (a request's verdict is about the issue it names — no signal bundle can single that out), and `model_from_request`, the first item-carried behavior-defining field, fenced by validation + the write-gated label + the pickup-time re-check. §16.10 lists exactly what the implementation touches, file by file.

## What today's `main` changed about it

- `outcome:delivered` is retired for new runs, so the successful end is an **approval park**, not a close — §16.5, S44/S46/S47/S49 and the `claude-in-review` label all follow from that.
- The simulator modeled the approval park only on the code-work path. The request task is the first agentic task whose *every* success leaves a PR, so the model gained the agentic mirror of it.
- "prework" is "code-work" throughout, the built-in task is `engine/…` (the pack namespace now belongs to the renamed `claudinite-*` packs), and §16.10's last line points at `packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md` rather than the retired `packs/core/scheduled-tasks.md`.
- My scenarios renumbered to **S44–S49**: `main` took S40–S43 for the triage split.

## Folders touched

- **`docs/tasks-dispatch/`** — §16 in `DESIGN.md`, amendment notes at §3/§5/§7, and §K in `SCENARIOS.md`.
- **`docs/tasks-dispatch/sim/`** — the request store, the adopt job, the item-aware precondition, the agentic approval park and the write-backs, plus the coverage rows.
- **`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/`** — the `claudinite-` prefix rule for feature packs, now citing the three packs that carry it.

## Verification

Six mutations were watched failing before the scenarios were believed — mark not consumed, eligibility skipped, disarm removed, model ignored, withdrawal ignored, and a PR-leaving run closing instead of parking. Each reddened exactly the scenarios that own it. Full suite green (2193), `check_the_world` 0 blocking, and `ci-work-scope` — the check that failed CI last time — exits 0.

## Not done here

Everything in §16.10: the engine code, `instructions.md`, the built-in task's own files, and the contract prose members read.

{"number":1059,"title":"claudinite-dashboard: give the published page a favicon","body":"Fixes #1058.

The dashboard linked no icon, so every deployment wore the browser's default blank tab — on the one page someone leaves open all morning beside a dozen others.

The mark is the pack badge's bar chart redrawn for a tab: thicker bars, no baseline rule (at 16px it closes into a smudge), same blue plane. It is its own file rather than a link to `badge.svg`, because the badge is a catalog asset the badge renderer owns and `build-site.mjs` deliberately does not publish it; the favicon's own comment says so.

Verified against a real run rather than the diff: `build-site.mjs` stages `favicon.svg` (and still omits `badge.svg`), `serve.mjs` returns it as `image/svg+xml`, and a headless Chromium loading the served page fetches it `200` — screenshotted at 16 / 32 / 64px and on a dark tab strip.

`packs/claudinite-dashboard/` — the new `favicon.svg`; the page and the site-root redirect link it; `serve.mjs` gains the `.svg` content type its table was missing.

No pack version bump: nothing about a member's tree changes shape, so there is no migration for a record to carry — the mount delivers the file on the next converge either way.

Pack tests 218/218 green; world conformance sweep 0 blocking, no advisory on this pack.

{"number":1056,"title":"Give every pack file one of the four sanctioned shapes","body":"Refs #1055. Two commits, two concerns.

## An agentless task's doc is a README

`task.md` is one thing: the spec an agentic task's session follows. Six tasks declared `agent_model: 'none'` and carried one anyway — `claudinite-growth/tasks/usage-fold` and all five `sheepdog/tasks/fleet-*` — each opening by saying it was *not* that ("This task runs no agent … the human-facing record of what that worker does"). Renamed to `README.md`, content untouched.

The file's presence is not inert: `routine-structure` judges any folder holding one against the routine prose↔script contract, and `discover.mjs` builds every work item's `taskPath` as `/task.md`, which `validate-dispatch` gates on existing — so the file was answering a question about a session that is never started. `task-md-only-when-agentic` (blocking, claudinite-growth) keeps the halves from drifting apart again; its `fix` is always the rename, never a deletion, because the content is the record of what the worker does.

Seen failing on exactly those six before the rename, silent after.

## The task contract leaves `RULES.md`

The rule added by #975 was "read this skill, and one line of its content". Every session in every declaring repo pays for that; the skill's own trigger description already fires on writing or changing a `task.mjs`. Dropped, with the pointer moved into the pack README where the contract is already described. **"Wanting a job to run in Actions" stays** — that one is a judgment call a session makes *before* it knows a skill is involved, so prose is where it has to live.

Nothing in the tree now names `scheduled-tasks.md`, and every check `doc:` field resolves — including `task-declaration-shape`'s, which #975 repointed.

## The static-site release standard becomes a skill

`packs/static-website/RELEASE.md` had the shape the task contract had before #975: 208 lines of authoring-time procedure reached only by following a link. It is now `skills/static-site-releases/SKILL.md` — moved whole, frontmatter added, wired into the pack's `skills` list, named in the README beside the three checks that judge against it, with the three `doc:` fields, the `RULES.md` pointer and the `bump-version` skill's link following it. No tombstone at the old path.

`packs/chrome-extension-release/RELEASE.md` is untouched here — its own change, since the call there is that the whole pack collapses into `chrome-extension`.

## Consumer safety

`consumer-safe-change` fired on the new blocking rule. It is answered with a **rehearsal fixture**, not a migration record: `aliases` rename a fixed path, and this rename is conditional on what a declaration *says*, which no record can express. The `code_work-env` fixture now carries its task's `README.md` — the shape a member holds afterwards — so the fixture is what proves the rule stays silent on it.

A member whose *own* local pack holds an agentless task with a `task.md` gets one blocking finding whose fix is a one-file rename: the migrate-through-the-check pattern `consumer-safe-changes.md` sanctions for artifacts canon cannot move. Canon's packs carry the check and the renames in the same vendored tree, so no member sees them out of step.

## Folders touched

- **`packs/claudinite-growth/`** — the new check and its wiring; the six-way rename's own task doc; the `RULES.md` rule out and the README's rules table, skills prose and check catalog updated; the rule stated in the `writing-tasks` skill; `belongs` renamed to "the task contract".
- **`packs/sheepdog/`** — its five fleet task docs renamed and the README's task table repointed.
- **`packs/static-website/`** — `RELEASE.md` → the `static-site-releases` skill, with the three checks' `doc:`, `RULES.md`, the README and a new Skills section following it.
- **`packs/basics/`** — the `bump-version` skill's link to that standard.
- **`packs-tests/rehearsal/`** — the fixture shape above.
- Versions bumped on all four packs; `packs/directory.GENERATED.md` re-rendered by its test.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 2186 pass, 0 fail.
- `check_the_work --changed --base origin/main` — exit 0.
- `check_the_world` — 0 blocking, 61 advisory (all pre-existing).
- The new check seen red on the real tree before the renames; every `doc:` field and moved link re-resolved against the tree.

## Findings across PRs #1082, #1081, #1077, #1076, #1067, #1071, #1068, #1070, #1063, #1060, #1062, #1011, #1059, #1056

Note on method: every one of these 14 PRs has **zero** review comments and **zero** review threads (`get_comments` and `get_review_comments` both returned empty for all 14) — these are single-session, self-merged AI-authored PRs with no back-and-forth discussion. So the evidence below is drawn from the diffs and the PR bodies' own stated reasoning, not from review pushback.

PR #1076: nothing durable (pure test-fixture cleanup, dropping a stale label from a fixture).
PR #1071: nothing durable (fixes an internal self-contradiction in a skill doc; narrow one-off wording correction).
PR #1068: nothing durable — its central fix ("judge mount freshness by stamp version, never by `stamp.updated` age") duplicates lessons already in RULES.md verbatim (`Judging whether a member is fresh`, `Judging whether Claudinite is current here`).
PR #1063: nothing new — this is the design-doc source for the same F26–F30 findings realized in #1067/#1082; already captured via #1067 below.
PR #1062: nothing durable — a straightforward "sweep every doc mention after a rename" fix, already covered by the existing `Renaming an entity — sweep for references in code and comments` rule.
PR #1011: nothing durable — design-only PR, precursor to #1063/#1067/#1082, no new content beyond what those land.
PR #1059: nothing durable (adding a favicon; pure feature work).

---

**Candidate lesson (PR #1067, corroborated by #1063's F30 ledger entry):**
- **Checking whether an actor may trigger a privileged automated action off GitHub's issue/PR payload** — read the actor's permission from the **collaborators-permission API** (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/collaborators/{u}/permission`), never the payload's `author_association`: `MEMBER` covers any org member regardless of repo permission, and `COLLABORATOR` includes read-only collaborators — both broader than push access.
- Evidence: `engine/scheduler/queue/signals/request.mjs` (via diff), comment: *"The permission API is the authority, never the payload's `author_association`: `MEMBER` is any org member whatever their repo permission, and `COLLABORATOR` includes read-only collaborators — both broader than push (F30)."* Also PR #1063 body: "F30: eligibility is **push permission read from the permission API**, not the payload's `author_association`." Test name: `S46 — the verdict is the PERMISSION, not the association (F30)`.
- Why durable: this is a concrete, easy-to-get-wrong GitHub-automation gotcha that generalizes to any future gate deciding "does this actor have push/write access" — the association field looks like it answers that question and doesn't.

**Candidate lesson (PR #1081):**
- **Renaming a canon pack** — sweep the pack's **abandoned vendored mount directory** under the old id as a property of the rename mechanism itself, not as something each future rename must remember. Vendoring replaces a tree per declared id; a renamed pack's old directory matches no id afterward and sits in the mount forever — and it is not inert, because the loader **canonicalizes** a mounted pack's own id on load, so the stale copy announces the *same id* as the live pack and the member silently runs two copies of it, one frozen at pre-rename content.
- Evidence: `updates/pack-update.mjs`, new `legacySpellingsOf(id)` helper and its comment: *"That copy is not inert — `discoverPacks` canonicalizes a mounted pack's own id, so the stale tree announces the SAME id as the live one and the member runs the pack twice."* Test: `engine-tests/.../pack-update.test.mjs` — *"a pack the canon renamed takes its old mount directory with it"*, driven through a real rename (`core` → `claudinite-lifecycle`), not a fixture map.
- Why durable: this is the "other half of a rename" that's easy to miss because code-side resolution (the rename map) makes everything *look* fixed while the member's actual mounted tree still holds a silently-colliding stale copy.

**Candidate lesson (PR #1081, second angle):**
- **Renaming a pack whose config a member writes into their own repo** — the rename map fixes *code-side* id resolution, but it cannot rewrite a member's **own already-committed config**, which converges on its own separate schedule (or never). A reader consuming that config must keep resolving **both** the new key and every legacy spelling explicitly, not assume the rename map alone makes old member-written keys readable again.
- Evidence: `packs/claudinite-fleet-sheepdog/fleet-config.mjs`: `cfg?.packConfig?.['claudinite-fleet-sheepdog'] ?? cfg?.packConfig?.sheepdog`, with comment: *"the legacy `packConfig` key is a member-written key that never converges at all... the old `packConfig` key is still read under the spelling it was written with."*
- Why durable: generalizes to any future pack rename where members store their own config under the pack's id — the rename map covers the engine's own bookkeeping but not data the member owns.
- Possible overlap: adjacent to the existing `Tightening a contract that member-owned files must satisfy` rule, but that rule is about contract *tightening*; this one is specifically about rename maps not reaching member-written data.

**Candidate lesson (PR #1060):**
- **Building a check whose job is to catch a thing being missing or wrongly renamed** — don't gate that check's own relevance on the single signal it's meant to validate. If the only gate is "does the orchestrator still have the expected `name:`", then the exact failure the check exists to catch (a renamed orchestrator) also makes the check **inert** at precisely the moment it's needed — the check that should say "rename it back" never fires. Use two independent signals, either sufficient, so at least one remains true when the other is the thing that broke.
- Evidence: PR body: *"gate only on the name and a repo that renamed its orchestrator loses every release check **including the one that tells it to rename it back**; gate only on the config and `cer/release-config`, whose whole job is a missing config, can never fire."* Implementation: `packs/chrome-extension/release-workflows.mjs`, `readShipsReleasePipeline` checks both the workflow `name:` text and `.github/release.config` presence.
- Why durable: a general trap in self-diagnosing/self-healing checks, not specific to chrome-extension releases — applies to any "detect misconfiguration X" rule whose detection is keyed on the same fact X corrupts.

**Candidate lesson (PR #1060, second angle):**
- **Writing a pack's own README/RULES** — never describe what a **neighbor** pack owns ("sits under X", "like firebase-release", a `## Boundary` section listing what neighbours cover). That's a second, driftable copy of what `ruleRoutingGuidance.excludes` (a machine-read field the pack directory already routes lessons by) states in one place. State only what *this* pack does not cover, never *who* covers it; keep only genuine procedure pointers (a link to a neighbor's skill/check), which the corpus already treats as legitimate.
- Evidence: PR body: *"A `barriers` probe... found **51 such crossings across 22 packs**... Purged. It is a second copy of what `ruleRoutingGuidance.excludes` already carries in one machine-read field... 22 references survive, all in the second class [procedure pointers]."*
- Why durable: a concrete, repeatable authoring-discipline finding (51 instances across 22 packs) about a specific failure mode — cross-pack narrative coupling — that will recur every time a new pack is authored beside existing ones.

**Weaker candidate (PR #1077) — flagging per instructions, possible duplicate:**
- **When more than one stage writes to the same human/agent-facing section** (e.g. adoption already binds a work item's "Context" scope; a later precondition also contributes to it) — let the earlier, authoritative writer's content stand and don't have a later stage restate the same fact; a reader told to treat a section as "the scope" has to reconcile two near-identical bullets that may or may not differ.
- Evidence: PR body: *"Adoption writes one when it creates the item; the precondition added another on the way through... Adoption's is the one that stands — it exists before any verdict — so the precondition adds none."* Diff: `engine/scheduler/queue/tasks/implement-request/task.mjs`, precondition drops its own `context:` entirely.
- Possible duplicate: adjacent to the existing `Referring to a value from more than one place` rule, but that rule is about literal stored values/constants, not about two independent code paths each rendering their own restatement of the same human-facing fact into a shared section. Flagging as a distinct angle rather than suppressing.

**Weaker candidate (PR #1056) — flagging per instructions, possible duplicate:**
- **Proving a consumer-safety fix is safe when the affected shape is conditional on a member's own declaration content** (not a fixed path) — a migration record can't express it (records are deterministic ops over fixed paths), so prove the new blocking check stays silent on that shape with a **rehearsal fixture** instead.
- Evidence: PR body: *"It is answered with a **rehearsal fixture**, not a migration record: `aliases` rename a fixed path, and this rename is conditional on what a declaration *says*, which no record can express."*
- Possible duplicate: overlaps with the extensively-documented existing rehearsal-fixture / real-corpus-testing material already in RULES.md (`Excluding files from the vendor set by pattern`, `Writing a check that scans the repo`), which already establishes "prove against the real tree / a rehearsal fixture, not just a synthetic clean case." The specific new wrinkle — *migration records can't express content-conditional renames* — may or may not be worth a standalone bullet; flagging for central dedup to decide.

No review discussion on any sampled PR — confirms these are unattended-agent-authored, auto-merged PRs with no human review comments. Findings below rely on diff + PR body only.

## Findings

**PR #1007: nothing durable** (possible duplicate — the "one entry not four checkboxes" point in this PR restates the already-captured rule "Writing a step a human must do by hand into an issue — a checklist whose items are mostly no-ops teaches the reader to skim it.")

**PR #1054: nothing durable** beyond one candidate below (the sim-fidelity point it makes is already covered verbatim by the existing "Building or extending a simulator for a stateful engine mechanism" rule).

- **Candidate lesson**: Asserting a mid-run invariant in a simulator/test — capture it at the exact moment the state holds, not after the run continues past it; a later re-check can pass vacuously once normal convergence has already cleared the evidence you meant to assert on.
  **Evidence**: PR #1054, `scenarios.test.mjs` S43 — "S43 re-queued before the task's first-ever item had ever left `task:blocked`, so it asserted over an item that never failed. The mutation check found it; it now asserts at the moment the lever is pulled, since by the end of the run the re-queued item has closed and taken every label with it."
  **Why durable**: Distinct failure mode from the existing "mutate-and-see-it-fail" and "model what the engine writes" rules already in RULES.md — this is specifically about *when* in a run to place an assertion, not what to assert.

**PR #975: two candidates.**

- **Candidate lesson**: A procedure doc reached only by following a link out of `RULES.md` or a check's `doc:`/`More:` line — if it's a how-to wanted at authoring time rather than prose every session should carry, convert it into a skill (frontmatter + description) invocable by description, not a doc chained through links.
  **Evidence**: PR #975 — moved `packs/claudinite-growth/scheduled-tasks.md` to `skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md` because it was "a procedure wanted at authoring time, not prose every session should carry, and today it is reached only by following a link out of RULES.md or a check's More: line." Verified mounted and offered by description in the next session.
  **Why durable**: General authoring-placement lesson, not tied to this one file. (Possible partial overlap with the existing "Writing a paragraph that explains how a mechanism works — not into RULES.md" bullet, but that's about mechanism-explaining prose, not about converting a linked reference doc into an invocable skill — flag anyway per instructions.)

- **Candidate lesson**: A check's `doc:` field is never opened by any tooling — it only renders into a finding's `More:` line — so a stale pointer left by a file move can sit broken indefinitely with nothing catching it; when moving or renaming a file, grep for and re-verify every `doc:` field against the tree by hand.
  **Evidence**: PR #975 — "`task-declaration-shape`'s `doc:` has pointed at `packs/claudinite-lifecycle/scheduled-tasks.md` since #1029 moved the packs — no file has been there since, and nothing caught it, because `doc:` is rendered into a finding's `More:` line and never opened."
  **Why durable**: A real, repeatable blind spot in the check-declaration mechanism; distinct from the sweep-discipline rules already in RULES.md (renaming-references, generated-file rules) because those don't call out that `doc:` specifically has no reader/validator.

**PR #1052: one candidate; rest duplicate.**

- **Candidate lesson**: Validating a required grant/permission ahead of time — a preflight probe is only as good as the environment it runs against; where the failure is conditional (a permission that only 403s under a specific condition, e.g. a private repo), a probe run where that condition isn't met reports false-positive success. Prefer attributing a real observed 403 to the permission that would fix it over guessing via an unrepresentative probe.
  **Evidence**: PR #1052 — "A preflight probe per permission... cannot be accurate where it matters: `Pull requests: read` fails only on a **private** member, so a probe against the enforcer's own repo would pass on a grant that later 403s... The 403 attribution gets the diagnosis without the guess."
  **Why durable**: Generalizable to any scope/permission validation design, not specific to this token.
  (The "state a multi-consumer requirement in one place" half of this PR duplicates the existing shared-constant/drift-guard rule.)

**PR #1053: nothing durable beyond a low-confidence candidate.**

- **Candidate lesson** (lower confidence): Moving a task's config source from one pack's declaration to another — keep reading the old pack's entry as a fallback and log which source supplied each key, so a member that hasn't re-declared config doesn't silently get a wrong default (e.g. a widened scope).
  **Evidence**: PR #1053 — "Reading only this pack's entry would silently widen a brief to every repo under the owner, so the reader falls back to that entry and every run logs which source each key came from."
  **Why durable**: possible duplicate of the existing "Extending what a copied stub reads — make the new config key optional..." bullet, but that's about stub files, not about a config *migrating pack ownership*; flagging per instructions rather than suppressing.

**PR #1051: two candidates; rest duplicate/product-specific.**

- **Candidate lesson**: Passing a diagnostic verdict out of a subprocess that may be killed at its own timeout ceiling — write it to the live output stream (stdout/stderr), never to a file: output already printed survives a SIGKILL, a file meant to be written at exit is never written at all if the kill lands first.
  **Evidence**: PR #1051 — the worker's triage marker is "Read from the output rather than a file, because it must survive the SIGKILL at `code_work_timeout` — output is echoed live, a file written at exit is never written at all."
  **Why durable**: Concrete, generalizable pattern for any subprocess-with-a-ceiling design; not stated elsewhere in RULES.md (which has adjacent but distinct rules about swallowed errors and about killing processes by pattern).

- **Candidate lesson** (lower confidence, possible duplicate): When introducing a finer-grained classification of an existing catch-all state, default anything an older/unaware writer produces (or a future writer's not-yet-known category) to the *most conservative* member of the new set, not the most lenient — here, a park with no recognized sub-label reads as `failure` (blocking) rather than one of the softer, non-blocking categories.
  **Evidence**: PR #1051 — "A park wearing no sub-label — every item an older engine left — reads as `failure`, so the compatibility direction is the conservative one."
  **Why durable**: Same shape as the existing "a dropped safety knob defaults to the most dangerous mode" rule but applied to the *opposite* direction (unclassified input → safest bucket rather than a removed parameter → most dangerous default); worth a line since the two are easy to conflate when designing a new field's default.

**PR #1048: one candidate.**

- **Candidate lesson**: Writing a generated title (a PR title, a notification headline) whose naive content scales with a variable-length list — collapse the list to a count in the title and keep the full per-item detail in the body; a title is a summary surface and grows unreadable exactly where a list of PRs/notifications makes every character compete for space.
  **Evidence**: PR #1048 — `updatePullText`: "THE TITLE IS A SUMMARY, THE BODY IS THE DETAIL. A title that names every moved pack grows with the number a member declares... so the packs collapse to a count and only the engine keeps its versions."
  **Why durable**: Possible duplicate/extension of the existing "budget generated content into a size-capped API field, two tiers" rule (currently framed around issue/PR *bodies*), but this is specifically about *titles* as their own compact-summary surface — worth flagging as the title-specific instance.

**PR #1047: nothing durable** (possible duplicate — "canonicalize on write as well as read, or a rename can never be called finished" is the same shape as the existing "Renaming a word that is also stored data... the decode side must rename them too" rule, just applied to a settings-stamp key rather than a usage-counter key).

**PR #1042: one strong candidate.**

- **Candidate lesson**: When an anchored-text/regex rewrite of a JSON declaration must reach a target that can sit inside a *nested* array within an entry object (e.g. `{"id": "barriers", "via": ["basics"]}`), the anchor cannot cross the nested closing bracket, so every element after such an object becomes invisible to it and the rewrite silently converges nothing on real data while a synthetic, non-nested fixture keeps passing. Parse and rewrite structurally instead (preserving key order/config/`via`/answers) — this is the one case where the standing "patch JSON as anchored text, never re-serialize" default should give way, because the correctness gap costs more than the formatting risk the anchored-text rule exists to avoid.
  **Evidence**: PR #1042 — the whole PR is exactly this: the 2026-08-19 pack-renames migration's regex "anchored on `"packs": [`... `[^\]]*?` cannot cross a `]`, and a real packs array holds entry objects with nested arrays... Both targets sit after those nested `]`. The anchor never reached them." Fixed with `applyPackRenames`, a structural JSON.parse-based rewrite. Also: "The fixture used an entry object with a plain `config` and no nesting — it spelled the same gap the pattern had... A fixture written from the same understanding as the code can only prove the matching; a real-tree replay is the only thing that can disagree." Companion PR #1047 found the same class of bug (regex-only compat) by the identical method — forcing a real member and reading its `main` back rather than trusting the exit code.
  **Why durable**: This is a genuine tension with an existing standing rule (`.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md`: "Editing a repo's JSON config — patch it as anchored text; never re-serialize... (portable → `repo-text-sweeps`)") and needs to be recorded as its boundary/exception, not just as a one-off bugfix. High confidence this belongs in the canon.

**PR #1027: one strong candidate.**

- **Candidate lesson**: A single timeout bound covering two different waits (whether something has appeared yet at all, vs. whether something already visible/in-flight will finish) reintroduces exactly the bug a prior fix closed for whichever side crosses the shorter phase's threshold while genuinely still working. Split the bound to match what each phase is actually waiting on, and size the "already in flight" bound from that work's own declared budget (e.g. the shortest relevant timeout among its callers) rather than an arbitrary round number.
  **Evidence**: PR #1027 — `landAttempt`/`LAND_TIMEOUT_MS` vs new `LAND_INFLIGHT_TIMEOUT_MS`: "Nothing visible yet... Waiting long buys nothing... A run we can see executing — the evidence is on its way... this gets its own budget... ceilinged by the prework budget it spends." Cost: "EdFringeNow... the poll gave up at 183s, 26 seconds before the second concluded... That is the standing ~24h offset #649 closed, reopened."
  **Why durable**: Names a repeatable design mistake (conflating "not yet started" with "in progress" under one clock) with a concrete resizing method; not stated anywhere in the current RULES.md.

- **Candidate lesson (paired with the above)**: A give-up/failure message for a bound that was hit must never read as a verdict on the work — "still running past the bound" and "verified failed" are different facts, and collapsing them sent a reader toward a wrong diagnosis (investigating repository settings for a repo whose CI was simply slower than the budget). Name what's still in flight explicitly, and reserve failure phrasing for an actually-observed failure.
  **Evidence**: PR #1027 — `failureSummary`: "'no successful run on its head sha' read as 'CI produced nothing green' on a member whose CI simply had not finished — which cost a wrong repository-settings diagnosis before #1026 was found. A timeout is a statement about the CLOCK, never a verdict on the runs."
  **Why durable**: General message-writing discipline for any timeout/give-up path, applicable well beyond this scheduler.

**PR #1028: nothing durable** (this PR is the code-side application of the freshness-by-version rule already captured verbatim in RULES.md via #1024 below, plus the already-covered "unknown is its own state, never zero" rule for a version that can't be parsed).

**PR #1013: one candidate; rest duplicate/already-captured (this PR is explicitly cited by PR-number in three existing RULES.md bullets: the legacy-spelling-maps-straight-to-today's-name rule, the persisted-counter-decode-rename rule, and the retiring-an-export-keep-it-callable rule).**

- **Candidate lesson** (moderate confidence): A test that derives its answer by walking git history (e.g., "which imports are still fielded, from trunk") must guard explicitly against a shallow clone and fail loudly rather than silently evaluate over whatever partial history happens to be present — a shallow checkout would otherwise make the test pass vacuously exactly when the real answer needs history it doesn't have.
  **Evidence**: PR #1013 — "Removing the shim turns `engine-pack-lane-shims.test.mjs` red (it derives fielded imports from trunk history, and needed `--depth=200` to be meaningful — it self-guards on a shallow clone and would otherwise have passed vacuously)."

**Source:** `2026-08-19T2241Z--issue-1069--37700002-7c1b-5c4c-b426-d8148614063d.jsonl`, issue #1069, session `37700002`.

**Evidence:** Owner asks (15:00) why GitHub Pages deploy is a raw workflow and not a Claudinite task. Agent answers with a permission/privilege argument ("a task structurally cannot reach an OIDC identity"). Owner pushes back (15:02); agent concedes at 15:03: *"You're right, and my previous answer overstated it… is wrong."* Same session, later (22:02–22:11), the agent leads with the same privilege-separation argument again for a related question (chrome-extension release) and gets shot down a second time; agent: *"You're right on both, and I've now led with the privilege argument twice and had it not survive."* The session then filed and landed issue #1069 / PR #1071 correcting the stated grounds in `packs/claudinite-growth/skills/writing-tasks/SKILL.md`.

**Candidate lesson:** Before repeating a design doc's stated justification for an architectural split (e.g. "task X can't have workflow Y's privileges"), verify each claimed ground against the current code (declared secrets, executor permissions) rather than reciting the doc — a stale rationale that hasn't been checked against implementation is exactly what a direct challenge exposes.

**Provenance summary (≤200 words, for issue #1069):** The owner asked twice why GitHub Pages deployment stays a raw GitHub Actions workflow instead of a Claudinite task, and pushed back hard on the agent's stock answer that a task "structurally cannot" hold the needed OIDC/permissions. The session then re-derived the actual reasons the carve-out exists (things a task genuinely cannot do structurally, distinct from privilege), filed issue #1069, and landed PR #1071 rewriting the false grounds in `writing-tasks/SKILL.md`. Lesson: verify a stated architectural rationale against current code before repeating it, especially once it has already failed a challenge.

---

### 2. Wall-time — CI status polled every ~8–20s despite declaring growing backoff sleeps that were never honored
**Source:** `2026-08-19T1657Z--issue-1030--994853fa-09cc-5b0f-b73e-6bf2e9fcd989.jsonl`, issue #1030 (PR #1052), session `994853fa`.

**Measured evidence (real timestamps from the log):**
- Episode 1 (16:43:12–16:46:18, ~3 min): 8 separate `mcp__github__pull_request_read`/`actions_list` polls, at intervals of 8, 16, 20, 23, ~35, 13, 10, 18, 11 seconds — while `sleep` commands of 100s, 120s, 90s, 240s were launched `run_in_background: true` in between and never actually waited out before the next poll.
- Episode 2 (16:55:07–16:56:31, ~1.5 min): 6 more polls at 10–20s intervals, same pattern, alongside declared 150–300s backoff sleeps.
- Net: ~14 near-immediate GitHub API polls across two CI-wait episodes in this one session, none of them separated by anything close to the declared sleep duration; the "backoff" text/duration is decorative.

**Candidate lesson:** When waiting on CI via a backgrounded `sleep`, don't re-poll the GitHub API again until that background command's own completion notification (or `ReadNotifications`) actually arrives — polling again seconds after declaring a growing backoff burns MCP tool-call budget for no wall-time benefit, since the outcome cannot change faster than the CI run itself.

**Provenance summary (issue #1030):** While waiting for CI on PR #1052 (two separate rebase/CI cycles inside one session), the agent repeatedly launched a backgrounded `sleep` (durations growing 90s→300s, following the house rolling-backoff convention) but then polled `pull_request_read`/`actions_list` again within 8–20 seconds regardless, both times, without ever waiting out the declared sleep. Across the two CI-wait episodes this produced roughly 14 near-immediate re-polls in under 5 minutes of real wall time. The CI itself still took as long as it took — no time was actually saved or lost — but the polling cadence didn't track the declared backoff at all, spending tool calls (and API rate-limit headroom) for no informational gain between polls. Worth a durable note: honor a launched background wait's own completion signal before re-checking, rather than re-checking on a fixed short cadence dressed up as backoff.

### 3. Recurrence (possible duplicate) — a new capability was built as a whole pack when it belonged in core scheduler code
**Source:** `2026-08-19T1740Z--issue-1010--5e8cca78-753a-5b26-b0d7-23a84212b4d4.jsonl`, issue #1010 (PR #1011), session `5e8cca78`.

**Evidence:** Agent designs and ships PR #1011 as a new standalone pack `claudinite-tasks-adhoc` implementing "label an issue → executor picks it up." Owner corrects hard: *"No no no, there's already the existing CCR, it should be invoked just like a regular task… these are all changes to the regular task scheduler and not a pack."* Agent: *"You're right — I built a pack around a gap the scheduler itself should [close]."* Substantial rework followed (new commits: "Design the ad-hoc request mode into the task scheduler (DESIGN §16)").

**Finding:** This is the exact failure class already documented in `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md` under "Starting a new Claudinite-facing capability… decide which distribution model it is before writing the first file" (citing #934, "one session paid it three times in a row"). This is a fresh recurrence of that same mistake, not a new lesson — **flagging as possible duplicate** rather than proposing new rule text, per the dedup instruction. Worth noting for growth-dedup/owner awareness that the existing rule isn't preventing recurrence, but that's outside this task's scope.

---

### 4. Recurrence (possible duplicate) — proposed a platform-setting change before verifying the actual cause
**Source:** `2026-08-19T1508Z--issue-1026--1e569218-f03c-5e13-8bae-551d1cea9458.jsonl`, issue #1026, session `1e569218`.

**Evidence:** A prior turn had filed `EdFringeNow#416` proposing a manual platform flag change on a member repo. Owner asks *"Why do we need EdFringeNow#416 to set a new manual flag? What changed?"* Agent re-investigates, finds the real cause was `land-pr.mjs`'s 180s poll giving up before a slower member's CI (which finished in 25s, well inside 3 minutes) was ever read, admits *"this was my mistake,"* withdraws and closes `EdFringeNow#416` as not-planned, and files/fixes the real bug as Claudinite issue #1026.

**Finding:** This is the exact failure class already documented: *"Diagnosing a member's maintenance PR that won't land — propose a platform-settings change only as a conclusion, never as a diagnosis."* **Flagging as possible duplicate.** The actual code bug fix (poll timeout too short) is a real, useful fix but belongs to the activity/commit lane, not a new conversational lesson.

---

### 5. Misunderstanding (hindsight window) — a reversed decision had to be repeated 5 times before it was durably purged from the repo
**Source:** `2026-07-19T2127Z--issue-364--8667dde0-cb49-5a8a-a903-b46c6c6e6b78.jsonl`, issues #360/#364, session `8667dde0`.

**Evidence:** Owner: *"Turn the local run-daily scheduling on, and for god's sake, eliminate that 'decision' that I want it off. **You've told me that 5 times and I kept telling you to change the decision.** Change the decision. Eliminate everywhere in the repo that says otherwise. canon-curation should move to local_packs. This is the new decision… Let's stop saying it won't move."* The session then explicitly planned a task ("Purge contrary statements; record the decision; update all references — every doc/comment that says canon-curation stays in packs/ or that local run_daily is off/experimental") and executed it (moved `canon-curation` to `.claudinite/local_packs/`, turned scheduling on, swept references).

**Candidate lesson:** When an owner reverses a standing decision, the fix isn't answering the immediate question — it's finding and purging *every* place in the repo (docs, comments, code defaults) that still states the old decision, and recording the new one durably where a future session will read it before ever asserting the stale version again. A decision corrected only in conversation, not in the artifact, gets recited back wrong indefinitely.

**Provenance summary (no issue post — this event is a month old, already resolved and merged; included for completeness/possible dedup-check only, not for posting):** The owner had apparently corrected the agent about `canon-curation`'s placement and local run-daily scheduling being on-by-default five separate times before it stuck, each time the stale "decision" text in the repo re-asserting itself to a later session. The final correction was blunt and explicit that the standing "off" default was wrong and needed eliminating everywhere, not just answered once more. The session responded by treating it as a durable-artifact problem: it planned and executed a purge of every contrary statement, moved `canon-curation` into `.claudinite/local_packs/`, wired local run_daily scheduling on by default, and reshaped the pack-independence check into generic barriers configuration — closing the loop so the next session couldn't recite the old decision again.

---

## No further keepers

The remaining fresh-window files (renames in #1022, needs-human label split in #1049, packs/RULES.md audit in #1055, docs review in #1010's later turns, various scheduled/routine-fired sessions #1014/#1018/#1019/#1041/#1046/#1064/#1065/#1075/#1079/#1080) showed normal execution — clarifying questions answered without rework, CI waits following the standard rolling-backoff pattern without the #1030 anomaly, `lgtm`-driven merges — nothing rising to a distinct, non-duplicate, evidence-backed lesson. Same for the remaining hindsight-window files (`issue-359`, `issue-366`, `issue-368`, `issue-373`, and the earlier half of `issue-349`) — routine feature work and one already-settled `/model` mid-session switch, no fresh friction beyond what's captured above.

**Measured evidence (real timestamps from the log):**

- Net: ~14 near-immediate GitHub API polls across two CI-wait episodes in this one session, none of them separated by anything close to the declared sleep duration; the "backoff" text/duration is decorative.

**Candidate lesson:** When waiting on CI via a backgrounded `sleep`, don't re-poll the GitHub API again until that background command's own completion notification (or `ReadNotifications`) actually arrives — polling again seconds after declaring a growing backoff burns MCP tool-call budget for no wall-time benefit, since the outcome cannot change faster than the CI run itself.

**Provenance summary (issue #1030):** While waiting for CI on PR #1052 (two separate rebase/CI cycles inside one session), the agent repeatedly launched a backgrounded `sleep` (durations growing 90s→300s, following the house rolling-backoff convention) but then polled `pull_request_read`/`actions_list` again within 8–20 seconds regardless, both times, without ever waiting out the declared sleep. Across the two CI-wait episodes this produced roughly 14 near-immediate re-polls in under 5 minutes of real wall time. The CI itself still took as long as it took — no time was actually saved or lost — but the polling cadence didn't track the declared backoff at all, spending tool calls (and API rate-limit headroom) for no informational gain between polls. Worth a durable note: honor a launched background wait's own completion signal before re-checking, rather than re-checking on a fixed short cadence dressed up as backoff.

What changed?"* Agent re-investigates, finds the real cause was `land-pr.mjs`'s 180s poll giving up before a slower member's CI (which finished in 25s, well inside 3 minutes) was ever read, admits *"this was my mistake,"* withdraws and closes `EdFringeNow#416` as not-planned, and files/fixes the real bug as Claudinite issue #1026.

**Source:** `2026-07-19T2127Z--issue-364--8667dde0-cb49-5a8a-a903-b46c6c6e6b78.jsonl`, issues #360/#364, session `8667dde0`.

This is the new decision… Let's stop saying it won't move."* The session then explicitly planned a task ("Purge contrary statements; record the decision; update all references — every doc/comment that says canon-curation stays in packs/ or that local run_daily is off/experimental") and executed it (moved `canon-curation` to `.claudinite/local_packs/`, turned scheduling on, swept references).
